images.title: Effectiveness of Targeted vs. General Medical Treatments
images.description: This diagram compares two medical treatment options for women over 50 with a specific genetic marker. Treatment A is shown as a targeted therapy with 92% effectiveness and low side effects, while Treatment B is a secondary option with 65% effectiveness and moderate side effects affecting multiple systems.
images.transcript: FILTER: WOMEN OVER 50 WITH GENETIC MARKER X; RANK 1; TREATMENT A; RANK 2; TREATMENT B; GENETIC MARKER X TARGETED; EFFECTIVENESS 92%; SIDE EFFECTS: LOW; OPTIMAL OUTCOME; EFFECTIVENESS 65%; SIDE EFFECTS: MODERATE; SECONDARY OPTION; SCIENTIFIC ILLUSTRATION DATABASE - VOLUME IV; WarOnDisease.org
images.socialCaption: We have the technology to target your specific genes with 92% accuracy, but we usually just give you the treatment that makes your hair fall out and your stomach hurt because it's cheaper. Science is marvelous. https://WarOnDisease.org #WarOnDisease #MedicalResearch
images.twitterText: We can target a specific gene with 92% accuracy, or we can just guess and hope your kidneys don't mind the collateral damage. https://WarOnDisease.org
images.linkedInText: Treatment A works almost perfectly. Treatment B works 'mostly' but adds several new problems to your weekly schedule. We currently spend more on perfecting ways to destroy buildings than on making sure everyone gets Treatment A. A fascinating choice by our species. https://WarOnDisease.org
images.speakerNotes: This slide illustrates the clear advantage of precision medicine. When we invest in research that allows for targeting specific genetic markers, we don't just increase effectiveness from 65% to 92%; we radically reduce the systemic side effects that plague traditional broad-spectrum treatments.
talkingPoints: Comparison of targeted vs. general treatment outcomes
92% effectiveness in targeted therapy vs 65% in general secondary options
Impact of precision medicine on patient quality of life through reduced side effects
images.altText: A comparative diagram showing two treatments for women with genetic marker X. Treatment A targets the marker directly with 92% effectiveness and low side effects. Treatment B is less precise, showing 65% effectiveness and moderate side effects across the body.
images.callToAction: Retweet
images.factCheckNotes: The data points are illustrative to represent the concepts of precision medicine vs. traditional therapy rather than a specific clinical trial result.

images.title: Comparative Cost Efficiency of Global Health Interventions
images.description: A logarithmic bar chart comparing the cost per Disability Adjusted Life Year (DALY) across four interventions. It demonstrates that the '1% Treaty' for medical research is significantly more cost-effective at $0.0018 per DALY compared to malaria bed nets ($89), GiveWell charities ($3.5k-$5.5k), and cancer screening ($20k+).
images.transcript: COMPARATIVE COST PER DALY (LOGARITHMIC SCALE) (Lower is better). COST PER DALY ($) (LOG SCALE). $100,000 ($10^5). $20,000+ Early detection programs. $10,000 ($10^4). $1,000 ($10^3). Top Charities: $3.50K - $5.50K. $100 ($10^2). $89. $10 ($10^1). $1 ($10^0). $0.10 ($10^-1). $0.01 ($10^-2). $0.001 ($10^-3). $0.0001 ($10^-4). CANCER SCREENING. GIVEWELL CHARITIES. MALARIA BED NETS. 1% TREATY (Timeline Shift). 50.3k:1 better than bed nets. Orders-of-magnitude difference in efficiency. $0.0018. INTERVENTION. WarOnDisease.org.
images.socialCaption: Humanity is remarkably talented at overpaying for things. We currently spend $20,000 to save a year of life that research could save for less than a fifth of a cent. https://WarOnDisease.org
images.twitterText: It turns out saving a human life costs $0.0018 if we fund research instead of just buying more tanks. But tanks have much cooler camouflage patterns. https://WarOnDisease.org
images.linkedInText: Most executives hunt for 5% efficiency gains. This data shows an intervention 50,000 times more effective than the current gold standard of global charity. The catch? It requires a long-term perspective, which is currently out of stock. https://WarOnDisease.org
images.speakerNotes: This chart uses a logarithmic scale to show the massive disparity in how we spend money to save lives. While malaria bed nets are famous for being high-impact, the '1% Treaty'—investing in accelerating medical research—is actually 50,000 times more cost-effective per dollar spent because it shifts the entire timeline of discovery for everyone.
talkingPoints: Logarithmic scale highlights that differences aren't just incremental, they are orders of magnitude.
The 1% Treaty costs approximately $0.0018 per DALY saved.
Traditional high-cost interventions like cancer screening are essential but inefficient compared to foundational research.
Accelerating the 'Timeline Shift' in research creates the largest ROI in human history.
images.altText: A bar chart on a logarithmic scale comparing the cost per Disability Adjusted Life Year (DALY). Cancer screening is over $20,000, GiveWell charities are around $4,500, malaria bed nets are $89, and the 1% Treaty for research is only $0.0018, making it 50,300 times more efficient than bed nets.
images.callToAction: Learn more about the 1% Treaty at WarOnDisease.org
images.factCheckNotes: The $0.0018 figure is a calculated projection based on the impact of shifting medical discovery timelines forward; traditional charity costs are based on 2020-era GiveWell and clinical data.

images.title: Redirecting Military Incentives Toward Global Health Outcomes
images.description: A complex flow diagram illustrating a proposed financial model where 1% of military spending ($27.2 billion) is redirected into a '1% Treaty Fund'. The chart shows how this fund distributes resources to pragmatic medical trials, investor returns via Victory Bonds, and political incentives to create a self-sustaining cycle of economic growth and peace dividends.
images.transcript:
Redirecting Competitive Incentives Towards Positive-Sum Health Outcomes

Military Contractors: Retain 99% of current budgets while redirecting 1% to fund global health security initiatives
1% Treaty Fund ($27.2B)
Pragmatic Trials (80%)
Patients/Pharma
Patients: Subsidized trial access, reduced healthcare costs, faster innovation. Pharma: Reduced R&D Cost
Reduced R&D Cost
Investor Returns (10%)
Bond Holders
Investors: VICTORY Incentive Alignment Bonds offer 272% long-term returns through health savings and growth
Political Incentives (10%)
Legislators
Politicians: ...gain reputation benefits, national security advantage, reduced defense pressure. Legislators: Political Support
Political Support
Peace Dividend Economic Growth & Stability
WarOnDisease.org
images.socialCaption: We've spent centuries perfecting the art of spending billions to turn people into dust. This plan suggests we try spending 1% of that on keeping them as people instead. It's a radical pivot, but the ROI on not being dead is surprisingly high. https://WarOnDisease.org
images.twitterText: We've mastered the logistics of global destruction. Surely we can manage a 1% shift into global health without the world ending. Or at least, ending slightly slower. https://WarOnDisease.org
images.linkedInText: Our current global security model is built on very expensive things that explode. This framework proposes we redirect just 1% of that toward 'not dying of preventable diseases.' It's a bold strategy for the quarterly reports, I know. https://WarOnDisease.org
images.speakerNotes: This diagram outlines the core mechanics of the 1% Treaty. By redirecting a fractional amount of military spending into a centralized fund, we can subsidize 80% of pragmatic clinical trials and provide a 272% return for bondholders. It transforms the defense industry's zero-sum competition into a positive-sum health outcome that benefits legislators, investors, and patients alike.
talkingPoints: Redirects 1% of military budgets to create a $27.2B medical research fund
Allocates 80% of the fund to pragmatic trials to lower drug development costs
Utilizes VICTORY Bonds to offer investors a 272% return driven by health savings
Creates a self-reinforcing 'Peace Dividend' through economic stability
images.altText: A flow chart showing how a 1% redirect of military spending creates a $27.2 billion Treaty Fund, which distributes money to medical trials, bond holders, and political incentives to foster economic growth and health.
images.callToAction: Learn more at WarOnDisease.org
images.factCheckNotes: The $27.2B figure represents a projection based on global military spending scales; the 272% return is a specific calculation within the VICTORY bond proposal framework.

Investor returns are projected at 272%, incentivizing private capital to back medical breakthroughs.

images.title: Comparison of Reactive and Proactive Drug Safety Monitoring Systems
images.description: This diagram contrasts the current reactive drug safety system with a proposed proactive model using automated Electronic Health Record monitoring. Using the Vioxx recall as a case study, it illustrates how shifting from voluntary reporting to automated signal detection could reduce detection time from five years to six months, preventing tens of thousands of deaths.
images.transcript:
CURRENT SYSTEM (Vioxx Example)
5 YEARS OF VOLUNTARY REPORTING
YEAR 5
APPROVAL (Year 0)
FAINT SIGNALS IGNORED
ADVERSE EVENTS UNDERREPORTED
Vioxx killed 38,000-55,000 people over 5 years... under the "safe" current system...
RECALL AFTER 38,000+ DEATHS
PROPOSED SYSTEM (Automated EHR Monitoring)
LIVES SAVED GAP
MONTH 6
APPROVAL (Year 0)
AUTOMATED EHR MONITORING
SIGNAL DETECTION
ALERT ISSUED
Proposed system uses automated EHR monitoring of all patients, detecting safety signals in months instead of years
SYSTEMIC CHANGE: Proactive surveillance replaces reactive reporting to prevent mass harm.
WarOnDisease.org
images.socialCaption: The current system for drug safety waits for thousands of people to die before noticing a problem. It’s a very patient system. #WarOnDisease #MedicalResearch #PublicHealth https://WarOnDisease.org
images.twitterText: Vioxx killed 38,000+ people because it took 5 years to notice the problem. We could do it in 6 months with automation. But why rush? https://WarOnDisease.org
images.linkedInText: Our current method for catching dangerous drugs is to wait for enough voluntary reports to pile up. This takes years and thousands of lives. Automated EHR monitoring could identify risks in months, but then we'd lose all that quality time with the status quo. https://WarOnDisease.org
images.speakerNotes: This slide highlights the 'Lives Saved Gap.' In the Vioxx case, the current system of voluntary reporting took five years to trigger a recall, leading to upwards of 55,000 deaths. A proactive system using automated EHR monitoring could have identified those same signals in just six months.
talkingPoints: Voluntary reporting is inherently reactive and relies on delayed manual input.

# **Abstract**

Representative democracy suffers from a fundamental principal-agent problem: elected officials systematically diverge from citizen preferences due to information asymmetry, special interest capture, and misaligned incentives. Meanwhile, direct democracy mechanisms reduce complex trade-offs to binary choices, losing crucial information about preference intensity. This paper introduces Wishocracy, a governance mechanism that addresses the democratic principal-agent problem by aggregating citizen preferences and creating accountability for elected representatives. The mechanism employs Randomized Aggregated Pairwise Preference Allocation (RAPPA), which presents participants with simple pairwise comparisons ('allocate $100 between cancer research and infrastructure') and aggregates millions of such judgments into preference weights that approximate utilitarian social welfare. Building on the Analytic Hierarchy Process [@saaty-1980] for cognitive tractability and collective intelligence research [@surowiecki-2004] for aggregation, RAPPA decomposes n-dimensional preference spaces into tractable binary choices while preserving preference intensity information. We present formal mechanism properties, computational complexity analysis, and empirical precedents from Porto Alegre's participatory budgeting, Taiwan's vTaiwan platform, and Stanford's voting research. Rather than replacing representative democracy at the municipal level, we propose a federal-first implementation: (1) documenting the gap between citizen preferences and actual federal allocations, (2) creating public "Citizen Alignment Scores" for elected officials, and (3) integrating with Incentive Alignment Bonds to channel electoral and financial resources toward politicians whose voting records align with aggregated citizen preferences. This approach treats Wishocracy as an accountability mechanism that makes representative democracy work better, requiring no authority transfer, only information provision and incentive alignment.
